text: Before pointing anything at these files, let's confirm exactly what's already there. This lesson is a quick inventory of the real S3 location and the real file contents the rest of this project builds on.

The Operations Manager's upload landed in northfield-raw-zone, the same raw-zone bucket IT already set up, under its own prefix: orders-raw. Inside that prefix are thirty-one files, one per day of August 2026, sitting flat — no date subfolders, no partitioning. That's the actual, honest state this data is in right now.

Each file is one day's order line items, exported straight from the on-prem SQL Server. Seven columns: order ID, order date, product category, product name, quantity, unit price, and customer region. That's everything needed to answer the stakeholder's question — category, quantity, and unit price are exactly what gets aggregated starting in Lesson 7.

There's no automated ingestion job behind this upload — no scheduled task, no success marker file, nothing checking completeness automatically. That machinery belongs to a recurring pipeline, and this is a one-time manual drop. So checking it is simple: aws s3 ls with the summarize flag, which prints a total object count and size — a fast sanity check that all thirty-one days made it in and nothing uploaded as zero bytes.

It's worth noticing what this layout is NOT. These files could have been uploaded already organized by date, but they weren't, on purpose. A flat prefix is the honest starting point for a one-off ask against a single month of data — and Lesson 8 comes back to this exact same prefix to show what changes, and why, once repeated access starts to matter.
With the files confirmed, next lesson points a Glue Crawler at this exact prefix and turns these thirty-one flat files into a real, queryable table in the Glue Data Catalog.
